**DATASCI 406 FA 26, Quiz 1.4**

**Name and Uniqname:**

## Question 1 (1 point)

You simulate $B = 999$ datasets under $H_0$ and find that **every** simulated
value of the test statistic is smaller than the observed $t_{\text{obs}}$.
What do you report? **Circle one.**

1. $\hat p = 0$
1. $\hat p = 1/1000$
1. $\hat p = 1/999$
1. $\hat p < 0.05$; the simulation cannot pin the value down any further.

## Question 2 (1 point)

$X_1, \ldots, X_{25}$ are independent draws from $N(\mu, 1)$; the statistic $T$
is the **sample median**; $H_0 : \mu = 0$ against $H_1 : \mu = 0.35$; and the
rejection region was fixed in advance as $T > 0.3$.

```{r echo = TRUE}
set.seed(406)
null <- replicate(20000, median(rnorm(25, 0.00, 1)))
alt  <- replicate(20000, median(rnorm(25, 0.35, 1)))
round(c(A = mean(alt),      B = mean(null > 0.3),
        C = mean(alt < 0.3), D = mean(alt > 0.3)), 3)
```

Which printed value is the **size** of this test, and which is its **power**
against $\mu = 0.35$? Write one label in each blank.

size $=$ \underline{\hspace{0.5in}} \qquad power $=$ \underline{\hspace{0.5in}}

## Question 3 (3 points)

$X_1, \ldots, X_{40}$ are independent $\text{Exp}(\text{rate} = \theta)$ with
$\theta$ unknown. The test statistic is the 25% trimmed mean
`mean(x, trim = 0.25)`, which has no convenient sampling distribution. The
observed data give $t_{\text{obs}} = 1.39$.

Suppose we have implemented a **two-sided level-0.05 test** of $H_0 : \theta = \theta_0$ against
$H_1 : \theta \ne \theta_0$, for one particular $\theta_0$ using a Monte Carlo hypothesis test.
The procedure is implemented as a function `test(t_obs, theta_0)` that returns
`TRUE` if the hypothesis is rejected and `FALSE` if the hypothesis is not
rejected.

Using this function, describe how you would
produce a **95% confidence interval for $\theta$**. Your answer must say both
(i) what you would compute, in enough detail that someone could code it from
your description, and (ii) why what you get is a 95% interval. You may suppose that $\theta$ is known to fall in some range $[a,b]$.
